---
title: "Exercises — Fragmentation and size control"
---

Pen and paper. Try each one before opening the **Hint**, and the hint before the
**Solution** — the reasoning is the point, not the answer.

Have the [NEB selection charts](https://www.neb.com/en/tools-and-resources/selection-charts)
open for the enzyme questions.

# Part 1 — Cutting

## E1. Pick the cut

For each goal, pick a fragmentation method and say which property of the method decides it.

a. Whole-genome sequencing of a human blood sample, 10 ng of DNA, PE150
b. Methylation at CpG-rich promoters in many patient samples, with the same loci in every sample
c. Which parts of the genome are open in primary human T cells, from 50 000 cells
d. Transcriptome of total RNA from a human cell line, with even coverage along the transcripts

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Ask three questions for each: what do I start with (DNA, RNA, chromatin), do I need the same ends
in every sample, and do I want the fragments to report on the sample?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. **Tagmentation or enzymatic fragmentation.** Low input and one tube decide it. Acoustic shearing
   at 10 ng works but loses more in handling.
b. **Restriction digest** (a CpG-cutting enzyme such as MspI), as in reduced-representation
   bisulfite sequencing. The deciding property is that every fragment starts at a recognition
   site, so the same loci appear in every sample.
c. **Tagmentation in nuclei** (ATAC-seq), or DNase I. The deciding property is that the cut falls
   where the chromatin is open, so the fragments are themselves the measurement.
d. **Metal-ion hydrolysis of the RNA before reverse transcription.** It is near-random, and the
   fragmentation happens before the cDNA is made, so coverage is not tied to the 3' end.
:::

## E2. The wrong DNA concentration

A tagmentation kit asks for 1 ng of human genomic DNA. Your absorbance reading gave 5 ng/ul and
you used 0.2 ul. A fluorescence assay later shows 1.3 ng/ul in the same stock. The library
trace comes out with most of the DNA below 150 bp.

Explain the result and say which reading to trust.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Tn5 cuts until it runs out of enzyme. What happens when there is more enzyme per molecule of DNA
than intended?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
The absorbance reading counts anything that absorbs at 260 nm: RNA, free nucleotides and
single-stranded DNA as well as double-stranded genomic DNA. The fluorescence assay is specific for
double-stranded DNA. The tube held 0.2 x 1.3 = 0.26 ng, a quarter of the intended 1 ng.
The enzyme was therefore in four-fold excess, every molecule was cut many times, and the
fragments are too short. Trust the fluorescence reading, and quantify tagmentation input with it
every time.
:::

## E3. RNA fragments that will not ligate

You fragment RNA with magnesium at 94 degrees, purify it, and try to ligate a 3' adapter
directly with T4 RNA ligase. Almost nothing ligates. Why, and what are two ways round it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Look back at the end chemistry in the nucleic-acids unit. What does a ligase need on the RNA's
3' end?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Metal-ion hydrolysis leaves a **2',3'-cyclic phosphate** on the 3' end and a **5'-OH** on the
5' end. The ligase needs a free 3'-OH on the acceptor, and the cyclic phosphate does not offer
one.

Ways round: (1) treat with T4 polynucleotide kinase, whose 3' phosphatase activity opens the
cyclic phosphate and gives a 3'-OH, and which also phosphorylates 5'-OH ends; (2) change the order
of the steps and make cDNA from intact RNA first, then fragment and ligate to DNA, accepting some
3' bias if you prime with oligo-dT.
:::

## E4. Bisulfite and adapters

You attach standard Illumina adapters to sheared human DNA and then bisulfite-convert it. The
library fails: nothing amplifies. A colleague suggests either methylated adapters or adding the
adapters after the conversion. Explain why the library failed and compare the two fixes.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
What does bisulfite do to an unmethylated cytosine, and what does that do to a primer binding
site that contains cytosines? Bisulfite is also harsh on DNA.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Bisulfite converts unmethylated cytosines to uracil, which reads as thymine. The adapter
sequences contain cytosines, so after conversion they no longer match the primers, and the
library does not amplify. The treatment also fragments DNA by itself, so much of the library is
destroyed before it can be amplified.

**Methylated adapters** keep their cytosines through conversion, but the DNA is still fragmented
and damaged after adapters have been put on. **Adding adapters after conversion** (post-bisulfite
adapter tagging) puts the fragile step first and the adapters last, so the adapters are never
exposed to bisulfite. The price is that the converted template is single-stranded and has to be
tagged by a different chemistry.
:::

# Part 2 — Size

## E5. Read length against insert

You run 2 x 150 paired-end reads. A library has three populations of insert: 90 bp, 250 bp and
500 bp. For each, say what the sequencer reads. How many bases of a 150 base read are adapter
for the 90 bp insert, and how much do the two reads overlap for the 250 bp insert?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
- **90 bp**: each read goes 150 - 90 = 60 bases into the adapter. That is 40 % of every read,
  and the same for both reads. The adapter must be trimmed.
- **250 bp**: the reads cover 300 bases of a 250 base molecule, so they overlap by 50 bases.
- **500 bp**: the reads cover 300 of 500 bases, leaving a 200 base unsequenced middle.
:::

## E6. Bead arithmetic

Your ligation reaction is 60 ul, cleaned to remove adapters, and you want to keep inserts of
roughly 300 to 500 bp with a double-sided selection at 0.55x and 0.7x.

a. How many ul of beads do you add in each step, and what do you keep each time?
b. Assuming the bead stock holds 20 % PEG, what is the final PEG concentration in each step?
c. A colleague computed the second addition as 0.15x of the supernatant. Which way does the
   edge move?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Both ratios are counted against the original 60 ul. The second addition is what is missing from
the total. Final PEG is the stock concentration multiplied by the beads' share of the total volume.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. First: 0.55 x 60 = **33 ul**; keep the **supernatant** (the long tail is on the beads and
   is discarded). Second: total 0.7 x 60 = 42 ul, so add **9 ul**; keep the **beads** and
   discard the supernatant.
b. First step: 20 x 0.55 / 1.55 = 7.1 %. Second: 20 x 0.7 / 1.7 = 8.2 %.
c. The supernatant is 60 + 33 = 93 ul. 0.15 x 93 = 14 ul, not 9, so the total is 47 ul of
   beads, 0.78x of the original sample. The ratio is higher, so the lower edge moves to
   shorter fragments and more short material is kept.
:::

## E7. PEG in the sample

You clean up 30 ul of a ligation that contains 5 % PEG with 24 ul of beads (0.8x), expecting the
same cut-off as 0.8x in water. The bead stock is 20 % PEG.

a. What is the final PEG concentration, and what is the equivalent ratio in water?
b. How many ul of beads would give the intended concentration of 0.8x in water?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
The final concentration is the total PEG divided by the total volume. In water, 0.8x gives
20 x 0.8 / 1.8 = 8.9 %.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. Total PEG: 30 x 5 + 24 x 20 = 630 units in 54 ul, so 11.7 %. In water, ratio r gives
   20r/(1 + r) = 11.7 %, so r = 1.4. The clean-up behaves like 1.4x, and keeps much shorter
   fragments than planned.
b. Solve (30 x 5 + V x 20) / (30 + V) = 8.9: 150 + 20V = 267 + 8.9V, so V = 10.5 ul, about
   0.35x. The cleaner choice is to remove the PEG first or dilute the reaction, then use the
   standard ratio.
:::

## E8. What went wrong

A double-sided selection of 0.6x then 0.8x is meant to give a 300 to 500 bp library. The trace
after the clean-up shows the right peak, but with a tail of 150 to 250 bp fragments, and a small
adapter dimer peak. The elution volume and the ethanol are fine. The bench notes say the second
addition was 16 ul to a sample that started at 50 ul. What happened, and what is the effect?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
The second addition should have been 10 ul (0.8 x 50 = 40 ul total, 30 ul already added). 16 ul
brings the total to 46 ul, or 0.92x. The higher ratio moved the lower edge to shorter fragments:
they bound the beads and were kept. That explains the shoulder at 150 to 250 bp and the dimer.
The fix is to count against the original volume.
:::

# Part 3 — Tricks

## E9. Counting cells with shear points

In an HTLV-1 infected T-cell clone assay, each integration site is sequenced from the junction
to a random shear point. Assume shear lengths from 150 to 450 bp can be resolved to 1 bp, so 300
distinct lengths, all equally likely.

a. Expected distinct lengths from a clone of 40 cells?
b. From a clone of 300 cells?
c. Which gives the worse count, and what are two ways to improve it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
The chance that a given length is missed by all n cells is (1 - 1/300)^n. Use
(1 - 1/300)^n ≈ e^(-n/300).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. 300 x (1 - e^(-40/300)) = 300 x (1 - 0.875) = **37.5**: a 6 % undercount.
b. 300 x (1 - e^(-1)) = 300 x 0.632 = **190**: a 37 % undercount.
c. The large clone. Two remedies: widen the range of shear lengths, which adds possible
   labels, or model the collisions statistically and recover the abundance from the observed
   length counts (the approach of Berry et al. 2012). Splitting the sample into aliquots before
   amplification is a third: it keeps each aliquot well below the number of possible lengths.
:::

## E10. Pick the enzyme, and spot the trap

You want a short, fixed-length tag from the 5' end of every transcript, cut from a linker you
attach to the cDNA. Use the NEB charts.

a. Which two properties of a Type IIS or IIG enzyme do you check first?
b. The enzyme's recognition site has 6 bases. Roughly how often will it occur inside a
   human transcript, and what does that do to your tags?
c. How do you make sure that only the cut next to the linker is read?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
A given 6 base site occurs by chance about once every 4^6 bases. Then think about what a streptavidin
capture could keep.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. The **cut offset** (how many bases from the site, which sets the tag length) and whether the
   cut is **sensitive to methylation** of the DNA you will digest. Also check the end it leaves.
b. About once every 4 096 bases, but many sites are degenerate or have the two possible
   orientations, so more often. A 2 kb transcript has a good chance of one internal site, which
   cuts it in the middle and gives a tag that is not from the 5' end.
c. Put a biotin on the linker and capture with streptavidin after the cut. Internally cut
   fragments lack the linker and wash away. Tags from the linker side are the only ones kept.
:::

## E11. Keeping a long molecule long

You want 50 kb reads from human blood. A good extraction gives you molecules whose breakage is
a Poisson process: each handling step puts, on average, 0.5 breaks into every 50 kb of DNA. The
protocol has four such steps: lysis mixing, a transfer, a purification and a tube change.

a. What fraction of 50 kb molecules survives all four steps intact?
b. If you cut the number of steps to two, what is it?
c. Which steps do you remove first?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. The probability of no break in one step is e^(-0.5) = 0.61. After four steps:
   e^(-2) = **0.135**, about 14 %.
b. e^(-1) = **0.37**, about 37 %.
c. The steps that put in the most shear: vortexing or vigorous pipetting first, then column
   clean-up and any syringe step. Use wide-bore tips, gentle inversion and, where possible, a
   single transfer.
:::

# Self-check

Answer without looking anything up.

1. Which methods in this unit give a random cut, and which cut where the sequence or chromatin
   decides?
2. Why does Tn5 fragment size depend on the amount of DNA?
3. Why is DNA stable in alkali while RNA is not?
4. Does a higher bead ratio keep shorter or longer fragments?
5. In a double-sided selection, which fraction do you keep after the first addition?
6. Why must the second addition be counted against the original sample volume?
7. Why does PEG in the sample change a size cut-off?
8. Why do random shear points act as molecular labels?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answers
1. Acoustic shearing, enzymatic fragmentation and metal-ion hydrolysis are near-random. Restriction
   enzymes, MNase, DNase I and (to a degree) tagmentation depend on sequence or chromatin.
2. Tn5 cuts until the enzyme is used up, so the more DNA per enzyme, the fewer cuts per molecule.
3. RNA has a 2'-OH that can attack the neighbouring phosphate; DNA has none.
4. Shorter ones: a higher ratio means more PEG, so shorter DNA binds too.
5. The supernatant. The long fragments are on the beads.
6. Because the final PEG concentration depends on the bead volume relative to the original
   solution: what you want is a total of 0.8x of the original sample, not 0.2x of what is left.
7. The beads respond to the total PEG concentration, and the PEG in the sample adds to what
   the beads bring.
8. Each molecule is cut at a different place, so reads from different cells have different
   lengths, while PCR copies of one molecule keep one length.
:::

# Going further

- Take a kit you use and write down, for each step, what the volume of beads is relative to
  the sample. Compute the final PEG concentration for each.
- Run your own bead ladder: a DNA ladder cleaned at 0.6x, 0.8x and 1.0x, then a trace for each.
  Compare to the curves in the deck.
